statement: Egg size (or initial reserve) covaries with the nutritional status of the mother.

scores.rationale: The corpus provides strong, multiple supporting references for the stylized fact that egg size / initial reserve covaries with maternal nutritional status. The core DEB maternal-effect rule—that reserve density at birth equals the mother's reserve density at egg formation, so well-fed mothers produce well-fed offspring—is stated explicitly across several foundational sources (snippets 9, 13, 15, 18) and empirically corroborated in Daphnia (6, 7) and Daphnia/copepod growth models (2). Several snippets, however, note exceptions where some species (poeciliid fishes, daphnids, Sancassania mites) produce larger eggs under poor feeding, and direct measurements (5, 13, 14, 16) show egg size/volume decreasing with increasing food—an inverse relationship that partly contradicts a simple positive covariation. Despite these documented exceptions, the dominant pattern affirmed in the DEB literature is that egg reserve covaries with maternal nutritional status, so the consensus is corroborative while acknowledging recognized counterexamples.

scores.rationale: Several snippets directly support the stylized fact that egg size/initial reserve covaries with maternal nutritional status. The strongest are [16] (Northern Lapwings: maternal mass and condition positively correlated with egg volume, with condition depending on food availability), [15] (Yellow Dung Fly: maternal adult feeding/nutritional status strongly affects egg size and reproductive output), and [14] (Sociable Weaver: egg mass varies with allocation, modulated by helper-mediated resource availability). Others ([3],[5],[6],[9]) provide moderate corroborating context linking nutritional/resource status to egg provisioning. Snippet [2] is partly contradictory, finding no relationship between fecundity/nutritional metrics and reproduction in lobsters, though it concerns fecundity more than egg size per se. Many snippets are neutral, focusing on egg-size effects on offspring or female-size–fecundity relationships rather than maternal nutritional status. Overall the corpus moderately and consistently supports the fact, with little direct contradiction.

scores.rationale: Multiple snippets directly and explicitly support the stylized fact. DEB-specific sources (Pecquerie et al. [9], Kooijman & Sousa [11], Sardi et al. [1]) state that offspring reserve density / egg size depends on the nutritional state of the mother (well-fed females produce offspring in good condition). Empirical works on Daphnia [6,7], copepod-style assimilate models [2], and bird/fish maternal-effects studies [16,17,19] corroborate that egg size or provisioning covaries with maternal condition or size. The main tension comes from snippets [5] and [14]: [5] notes some species produce larger eggs under poor feeding conditions (an inverse relationship in certain taxa), and [14] found no link between fecundity/egg content and nutritional metrics in lobsters. These show the covariation is not universal in sign, but they do not deny that egg size covaries with maternal nutritional status—if anything they confirm a relationship exists, just sometimes inverse. Overall the evidence is strong and consensus is corroborating, with limited and explicable conflict.
